documents: Yang et al. (2022), Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL099886, published paper (PDF, 10 pages; Supporting Information not supplied)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (these coincide with the printed 'n of 10' journal pages)

entry.evidence: the opening mechanism of the Japan Sea, a representative example of a virtually intact continent-ocean back-arc system, is still unclear and under debate

sequences.source_document: Yang et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: The authors pose the unresolved question of what mechanism opened the Japan Sea back-arc basin.
steps.quote: the opening mechanism of the Japan Sea, a representative example of a virtually intact continent-ocean back-arc system, is still unclear and under debate

steps.action: The authors list published rival mechanisms: small-scale mantle-wedge convection (Toksöz & Bird), ascending convection with trench retreat (Uyeda & Kanamori), the paleomagnetic fan-shaped 'double door' rotation (Otofuji et al.), and the dextral strike-slip pull-apart model (Lallemand & Jolivet).
steps.quote: two driving mechanisms: small-scale convection in mantle wedge induced by descending lithosphere

steps.action: The authors choose Pn attenuation tomography as a probe of uppermost-mantle thermal structure, citing the premises that attenuation is mainly temperature-sensitive and that Pn samples the top tens of km below the Moho.
steps.quote: we conduct the Pn attenuation tomography beneath the Japan Sea and surrounding areas, and the results are used to detect the thermal structure

steps.action: The authors compile vertical-component waveforms of natural earthquakes and six North Korean nuclear explosions from CNDSN, GSN and F-net, window the Pn phase and noise, and select data with SNR at least 2.0.
steps.quote: We collected 29,232 vertical-component waveforms from 479 seismic events recorded at 242 stations

steps.action: The authors fit a Pn geometric spreading model and jointly invert single- and double-station amplitudes with LSQR at each of 42 frequencies (method of L. F. Zhao et al. 2015), giving a broadband Qp model with about 1°×1° resolution.
steps.quote: the single- and double-station data are jointly inverted by the least squares orthogonal factorization (LSQR) method

steps.action: The authors check the inversion uncertainty: amplitude residuals are near-Gaussian, and bootstrap resampling of the data set gives low standard deviations (Figures S9, S10).
steps.quote: The uncertainty from the observations was examined by resampling the original data set using bootstrapping technique

steps.action: The authors test the recovery of the tomography with 1°×1° checkerboards and three synthetic models resembling the real anomalies (Figures S8, S11, Text S2).
steps.quote: The reliability and robustness of the observed anomalies were further checked by using checkerboard test and synthetic model tests.

steps.action: The authors compare the low-Qp anomalies under the intraplate volcanoes and the Japan Sea margins with published low Pn, S-wave and Rayleigh-wave velocities, and the weak attenuation at the Japan Trench with high Pn velocity.
steps.quote: which are consistent with low phase velocities of Rayleigh waves in the 40–80 s period

steps.action: The authors interpret the low-Q anomalies as hot mantle material rising in branches to feed the Changbaishan, Jingpohu and Ch'uga-Ryong volcanoes, then flowing from Northeast Asia toward the NW and SW edges of the Japan Sea.
steps.quote: Hot mantle materials revealed by low Qp values seem to flow from Northeast Asia to the northwestern and southwestern edges of the Japan Sea

steps.action: The authors compare the strikes of the low-Q belts with published Pn anisotropy fast directions and shear-wave splitting, and with the rollback directions of the Pacific and Philippine Sea slabs, and infer laterally divergent flow.
steps.quote: a laterally divergent pattern of mantle flows can be confirmed by strong Pn attenuations stretched from Northeast Asia to the Japan Arc

steps.action: The authors compare published basalt and volcano ages (NE China, Sikhote-Alin, Japan Sea basement, Changbaishan, Ulleung) with the inferred direction of mantle flow.
steps.quote: The age distribution of these basalts are consistent with the divergent pattern of mantle flow.

steps.action: The authors compare the attenuation pattern with published crustal-thickness surveys: strong attenuation lies over thickened crust in the Tsushima Basin and western Japan Basin, and weak attenuation under the Yamato Basin matches OBS high velocities; they infer crustal thickening by mantle-derived melt.
steps.quote: The hot mantle flows seem to provide a large amount of molten material to form a thick igneous crust in the Tsushima Basin

steps.action: The authors argue that a single small-scale convection or ascending convection in the mantle wedge cannot by itself produce rotational opening.
steps.quote: is enough to rotationally open the Japan Sea

steps.action: The authors match the two attenuation-constrained flows to the paleomagnetic counterclockwise and clockwise rotations of the two Japan Arc blocks (Otofuji et al. 1985) and to the retreat directions of the two plates.
steps.quote: Two regional mantle flows constrained by strong Pn attenuation remarkably coincide with the counterclockwise and clockwise rotations of the two microplates of the Japan Arc

steps.action: The authors protect the link between present-day attenuation and Miocene opening by adding the auxiliary assumption that the current incipient closure has not erased the flow pattern.
steps.quote: the closure of the Japan Sea might not significantly change the mantle flow patterns

steps.action: The authors keep the 'double door' model: divergent mantle flows, driven by divergent Pacific and Philippine Sea slab rollback, pushed the Japan Sea open rotationally (Figure 3e).
steps.quote: The Japan Sea tends to open rotationally like a double-sided door, possibly pushed by divergent mantle flows during the Miocene and Pliocene

tree.answer: Opening mechanism of the Japan Sea, read from uppermost-mantle thermal structure
No; thermal structure inferred from Pn attenuation tomography
Explain a past opening event from present traces
Yes; small-scale convection, ascending/rollback convection, double door rotation, pull-apart
Not derived; only qualitative matching of flow orientation
Found: archived earthquakes and explosions; past opening known only from traces
Tomography survives bootstrap, checkerboard and synthetic tests; interpretation consistent with independent data sets
Double door opening by divergent mantle flows kept as best explanation
Not documented; no review file supplied

end.claim: The Japan Sea opened rotationally like a double-sided door, likely pushed during the Miocene–Pliocene by two divergent uppermost-mantle flows imaged as low-Q belts and driven by the divergent rollback of the Pacific and Philippine Sea slabs.

decisive_move.sentence: The broadband Pn Qp tomography revealed the two low-Q belts whose strikes anchor every later comparison; without it there would be no mantle-flow pattern to match against the paleomagnetic rotations.

gates.evidence: Attenuation was chosen because it is temperature-sensitive and the double door model was stated in the introduction, but the data were compiled from archives without a hypothesis-specific design. The orientation of the low-Q belts could have disagreed with the anisotropy and the rotations, but no quantitative prediction or rival forecast was computed. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: waveforms of six North Korean underground nuclear explosions used as sources

limits: No review file, discussion, or Supporting Information was supplied. The checks in Figures S8–S11 and Text S1–S2 are known only from the main-text summary. The Acknowledgments thank an editor and two reviewers, but what they changed is not recorded, so no review sequence is coded. The pull-apart rival (Lallemand & Jolivet 1985) is introduced but never explicitly tested or excluded. The exclusion of single-convection models is argued, not tested against computed predictions. The step from present-day attenuation to Miocene flow rests on the auxiliary in step 15, which is not tested. Inference: the temperature-only reading of attenuation (against melt or water content) is assumed from the literature and not checked here. The processing choices (SNR 2.0, 0.7 km/s window, geometric spreading model) are not varied in the main text. The corroborating data (anisotropy, shear-wave splitting, volcanic ages, crustal surveys, paleomagnetism) are all from other studies. Sub-claim statuses: the broadband Qp model is estimate_with_resolution (1°×1°, bootstrap and synthetic tests); the branched feeding of the intraplate volcanoes by hot mantle material is best_explanation; the crustal thickening in the Tsushima Basin and western Japan Basin by mantle-derived melt is best_explanation. The paper says the divergent flow 'can be confirmed', but the coded status is best_explanation because no decisive test was performed.

disagreements.target: The usual attribution of back-arc opening to rollback of a single subducting slab (Pacific plate)
disagreements.support: The coeval Philippine plate subduction, the arcuate volcanic zone, and the two divergent low-Q belts imply two plates' rollback.
disagreements.quote: its opening is unlikely only resulted from the subduction of the Pacific plate

disagreements.target: Single small-scale convection (Toksöz & Bird 1977) or ascending convection (Uyeda & Kanamori 1979) as the opening mechanism
disagreements.support: These mechanisms cannot by themselves produce the paleomagnetically documented rotational opening, whereas two divergent flows match both rotations.
disagreements.quote: However, neither single small-scale convection (Toksöz & Bird, 1977)

disagreements.target: The view that the Yamato crust formed mainly by extension of continental crust (Nakahigashi et al. 2015; Tamaki et al. [...]
disagreements.support: Citing D-type basalts with hotter melting conditions (Hirahara et al. 2015), the authors suggest an added mantle thermal contribution.
disagreements.quote: the crustal thickening in the Yamato Basin may also be slightly influenced by the high-temperature mantle materials from the magmatic arc

alternatives_considered.reason: velocity also depends on partial melting, magnesium content and garnet/olivine ratio, while attenuation is mainly affected by temperature and is more sensitive to heat sources

alternatives_considered.chosen: divergent mantle flows from two slabs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: single small-scale convection (Toksöz & Bird 1977); ascending convection (Uyeda & Kanamori 1979)
alternatives_considered.reason: neither alone is enough to rotationally open the Japan Sea

alternatives_considered.chosen: divergent slab pull/rollback of both Pacific and Philippine Sea plates
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Pacific slab rollback along a curved hinge line (Martin 2011)
alternatives_considered.reason: the two flows coincide with the two block rotations and with the retreats of both plates
